title: AI Strategy & Portfolio
subtitle: Turn business strategy into a value-ranked AI portfolio
summary: Build an enterprise AI strategy, find high-value use cases, sequence bets, and distinguish transformative initiatives from automation theater.

lessons.title: Strategy before tooling
lessons.body: Start from company strategy: revenue growth, margin, customer experience, speed, risk, and strategic differentiation. AI initiatives should map directly to measurable enterprise objectives.

lessons.title: Use-case discovery
lessons.body: Use process mapping and value-stream analysis to identify opportunities in decision support, content, software development, operations, customer service, knowledge work, forecasting, and autonomous workflows.

lessons.title: Portfolio scoring
lessons.body: Score use cases on strategic value, financial value, feasibility, data readiness, adoption difficulty, risk, time-to-value, and option value. Avoid a single ROI metric that hides strategic importance or risk.

objectives: Tie AI work to enterprise KPIs

quiz.q: An insurer's objective is faster claims resolution without more reopenings. A summarizer cuts draft preparation time in one supervised team. Which claim is currently most defensible in the enterprise strategy?
options: The pilot establishes faster claims resolution because drafting is a necessary step in every claim.
The pilot improved draft preparation in its tested scope; resolution time and reopenings still need comparative measurement.
The pilot establishes enterprise productivity because supervision reduced the risk of incorrect summaries.
The pilot establishes a cash saving because adjusters need fewer minutes to prepare each draft.
quiz.explanation: Task-level timing supports a narrow claim, while elapsed resolution time, reopening rates, and cash effects need their own evidence. A comparison and countermeasure prevent a local efficiency gain from being mistaken for the enterprise objective.

quiz.q: A service firm plans Canada and EU pilots using customer records. Regional privacy and legal owners are named, but neither live-data scope is authorized. A redacted design study is already permitted. Which funding sequence best prevents an investment commitment from presuming data-use permission?
options: Fund both live-data pilots, have regional owners classify each use, and make only production scale conditional on regional authorization and evidence gates.
Fund the Canadian live-data pilot plus an EU design study, have both regional owners classify uses, and obtain Canadian authorization at its first benefit review.
Fund the EU live-data pilot plus a Canadian design study, have both regional owners classify uses, and obtain EU authorization after its integration tests pass.
Fund the permitted design study, have regional owners classify each use, and make each live-data pilot conditional on its own authorization and evidence gate.
quiz.explanation: The permitted study can generate design evidence without assuming authority to use customer records. Regional classification and authorization must shape the live-data pilots before those commitments proceed; naming owners and adding later scale gates does not authorize the earlier use.

quiz.q: A pilot frees 2,000 annual staff hours after review, but headcount and spending will remain unchanged. The sponsor plans to use the hours to reduce backlog. How should the CFO-facing strategy describe the benefit?
options: Capacity released, with backlog outcomes measured separately and implementation and operating costs included.
Cash savings at the full loaded hourly rate, with backlog improvement recorded as an additional benefit.
Revenue improvement at the full loaded hourly rate, with operating costs charged to the platform budget.
No measurable benefit until staff spending falls, with released hours excluded from the investment case.
quiz.explanation: Released hours can support a real capacity or service case without being realized cash savings. The sponsor must show what the capacity produces, and the full cost still belongs in the comparison.

quiz.q: A spare-parts service takes a median three days to fulfill an order. Staff spend 12 minutes classifying it, but an approval handoff typically adds two days of waiting. A classifier can cut classification to four minutes; the business target is next-day fulfillment. What should discovery recommend?
options: Prioritize the classifier and use its 67% touch-time reduction as the forecast improvement in elapsed fulfillment time.
Combine the classifier and handoff changes in one pilot, attributing any fulfillment improvement to the classifier's measured touch-time gain.
Test the approval handoff against the fulfillment target, and assess the classifier separately for the capacity released by its eight-minute reduction.
Defer the classifier until the approval handoff disappears, excluding its capacity benefit from consideration while elapsed time remains high.
quiz.explanation: The two-day wait dominates elapsed time, so an eight-minute touch-time gain cannot establish next-day fulfillment. The classifier may still have a capacity case, while a separate handoff test targets the actual service constraint and makes attribution clearer.

quiz.q: A team handles 72,000 requests yearly. The target drafting step applies to 40% of them, and expected adoption is 75% of eligible requests. Draft assistance saves six minutes but adds two minutes of review per adopted request. Assuming these are the only time effects, how much annual capacity is released?
options: 2,160 hours.
1,440 hours.
1,920 hours.
4,800 hours.
quiz.explanation: There are 72,000 × 0.40 × 0.75 = 21,600 adopted requests, each releasing four net minutes. That yields 21,600 × 4 / 60 = 1,440 hours; omitting review or adoption overstates the benefit.

quiz.q: Adviser search could produce $300,000 yearly value, but conflicting source versions make its benefit estimate uncertain. The next gate must establish whether current authorized sources can support useful answers. A $20,000 sampled source-and-workflow test can answer that; full cleanup costs $180,000. A ready FAQ pilot costs $15,000 with only $10,000 expected yearly value and cannot answer the search question. Which discovery spend best addresses the decision now?
options: Fund the $20,000 sampled test, then use its result to decide whether cleanup and a search pilot warrant further investment.
Fund the $180,000 cleanup now, then test search usefulness once the source-version dependency has been removed.
Fund the $15,000 FAQ pilot first, then use its adoption results as the confidence measure for the adviser-search benefit estimate.
Defer both search and FAQ, holding the budget until the $300,000 estimate can be verified from existing records alone.
quiz.explanation: The sampled test buys the specific evidence needed at lower cost than committing to full cleanup. The ready FAQ pilot tests a different workflow, while waiting for existing records cannot resolve an uncertainty that requires observing source-supported search use.

quiz.q: A CAIO has $1 million. The mandate requires realizing the proven service gain this quarter and obtaining adviser-search evidence next quarter. Service scale costs $550,000; a search experiment costs $250,000 after a $200,000 shared permissions foundation. Each takes a full quarter. A separate platform team can build the foundation, while the two use-case specialists can implement only service or search in any quarter. Search begins only after the foundation is complete. Which feasible staging fits both deadlines?
options: Build the foundation this quarter, run search next quarter, and schedule service scale in the following quarter.
Scale service this quarter, build the foundation next quarter, and run search in the following quarter.
Build the foundation this quarter, scale service next quarter, and run search in the following quarter.
Scale service and build the independently staffed foundation this quarter, then run search next quarter.
quiz.explanation: Service needs the specialist slot this quarter, while the separate platform team can prepare the search dependency in parallel. Search can then use the next quarter's specialist slot; the other feasible sequences miss the service deadline, the search deadline, or both.

quiz.q: Search outranks routing under the original weights, but their ranking reverses when more weight goes to data readiness. Search's broad-access permissions are unresolved, although a redacted-corpus discovery test is authorized. Routing meets a capped-pilot gate. Scale funding needs stronger evidence for either. What is the best current allocation?
options: Fund a full search pilot on the original ranking, and ask its sponsor to resolve broad-access permissions before the first customer uses it.
Fund only the search discovery test, postponing the qualified routing pilot until the committee agrees on a ranking that survives every weight change.
Fund a capped routing pilot and an authorized search discovery test, with separate evidence and permissions gates before further commitments.
Fund equal pilot budgets for both candidates, restricting search to redacted data and assuming routing's existing pilot evidence covers its scale gate.
quiz.explanation: The rank reversal makes the allocation sensitive to assumptions, while each candidate has a different authorized next stage. A routing pilot and limited search discovery buy useful evidence without extending unresolved permissions or confusing pilot readiness with scale approval.

quiz.q: Candidates A and B meet all eligibility gates. Their strategy, value, feasibility, data-readiness, and adoption scores are A: 5, 3, 4, 2, 4 and B: 3, 4, 3, 5, 4. Original weights are 30%, 25%, 20%, 15%, 10%. Move ten percentage points from strategy to data readiness, holding the other weights fixed. What happens to their weighted ranking?
options: A leads 3.75 to 3.65 originally; B leads 3.85 to 3.45 after the change.
B leads 3.65 to 3.55 originally; A leads 3.95 to 3.45 after the change.
A leads 3.75 to 3.65 originally; A still leads 3.95 to 3.45 after the change.
A leads 3.75 to 3.65 originally; they tie at 3.65 after the change.
quiz.explanation: Original totals are A = 1.50 + 0.75 + 0.80 + 0.30 + 0.40 = 3.75 and B = 0.90 + 1.00 + 0.60 + 0.75 + 0.40 = 3.65. The new weights give A 3.45 and B 3.85, revealing sensitivity to the relative emphasis on strategy and data readiness rather than a settled ordering.

homework: Build a 12-use-case AI portfolio for a hypothetical company. Rank it using a transparent scoring model and select 3 lighthouse use cases, 5 scale candidates, and 4 experiments.
